pr_title: don't cancel container stop when cancelling context
pr_body:
- relates to https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/43206
- fixes https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/45731


Commit 90de570cfa5f6de0b02bdf2e794627fbf5b0dfc8 passed through the request context to daemon.ContainerStop(). As a result, cancelling the context would cancel the "graceful" stop of the container, and would proceed with forcefully killing the container.

This patch partially reverts the changes from 90de570cfa5f6de0b02bdf2e794627fbf5b0dfc8 and breaks the context to prevent cancelling the context from cancelling the stop.

issue_context.title: Issue with containerStop and long running tasks prematurely exiting
issue_context.body:
### Description

It seems that behavior has changed in docker 23+ in regards to containerStop and stopping long running containers via the API.  

Current behavior it seems when sending a POST to /stop?t=3600 the connection doesn't return a 204 until the container has fully stopped, so the connection in theory stays open for an hour.  If this connection is dropped then the container is killed.

Here's an example log of initiating the request and cancelling the curl.
```
Jun 12 15:24:41 dg11 dockerd[1263909]: time="2023-06-12T15:24:41.686151349Z" level=debug msg="Calling POST /v1.41/containers/1e70fb6382cb/stop?t=3600"
Jun 12 15:24:41 dg11 dockerd[1263909]: time="2023-06-12T15:24:41.686276060Z" level=debug msg="Sending kill signal 15 to container 1e70fb6382cb3d323f92ba2477d9430ea870f341e61af5623d02dc5056d6af7e"
Jun 12 15:30:52 dg11 dockerd[1263909]: time="2023-06-12T15:30:52.095812601Z" level=info msg="Container failed to exit within 1h0m0s of signal 15 - using the force" container=1e70fb6382cb3d323f92ba2477d9430ea870f341e61af5623d02dc5056d6af7e
Jun 12 15:30:52 dg11 dockerd[1263909]: time="2023-06-12T15:30:52.095878637Z" level=debug msg="Sending kill signal 9 to container 1e70fb6382cb3d323f92ba2477d9430ea870f341e61af5623d02dc5056d6af7e"
```
Docker 20.10 seems to return the 204 status code before the container is stopped, as our nomad client times out sending the POST request on docker 23+. 

### Reproduce

Start a long running container that emulates something like Haproxy spinning down open connections and tell it to stop.

```
curl -v --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock -X POST http://localhost/v1.43/containers/1e70fb6382cb/stop?t=3600
```
If you cancel the curl request the container will be killed immediately.

This is the client code we initially noticed the bug with, on docker 23+ the request times out, on 20.10 our stop behaves as normal.  https://github.com/fsouza/go-dockerclient/blob/main/container_stop.go
```
### Expected behavior

Is this the expected behavior of this endpoint?

I plan on also opening an issue with the nomad team as well as this is the client I originally noticed the issue with, but wanted to see if this was expected behavior or not as it seems to have changed between docker versions.

comments:
Thanks for reporting; I see where the issue is, and working on a fix.


It looks like this was introduced in https://github.com/moby/moby/commit/90de570cfa5f6de0b02bdf2e794627fbf5b0dfc8 (https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/43206), which propagated the context.

Before that change, the `daemon.containerStop()` would use a local context, but the above propagated the context from the request.

To problem here is that the existing code didn't consider that that context could be cancelled, and the code at these lines would return early if the container exited successfully, but proceed with the other code if that was not the case;
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/4bef3e9ed39493daec14c6432ceb57f78fb7bded/daemon/stop.go#L84-L87

That code didn't take a `context.Cancelled` into account, and interpreted it as "something went wrong", continuing to "force killing" the container.

oh, hm, I just started working on the fix, but now realised that in the old case, the stop would continue to run even when the client detached (so would never be canceled once requested). Slightly wondering now if that was intentional, or something in the original implementation (either one could make sense if the request was cancelled before completed).

Awesome thank you for working on this!  

This is where I was getting stuck,  I wasn't sure what the desired behavior is.  Currently on 20.10 our client ( nomad ) would POST to the endpoint and seemingly receive back a 204 letting our scheduler know that the container received our graceful shutdown.  I believe our job scheduler is checking if the container has stopped and then after the timeout period i'm assuming our nomad client would send a kill request ( I can try to verify this better if needed ).  I'm not sure how this behavior is with kubernetes and other job schedulers that use docker.

Yes, I think this is one of those cases where the intended behavior of the API was never fully documented (we improved in that area, but there's a lot of things from very early on in the project that sometimes have to be reverse engineered to document (or codify) things). Some of these are more complicated as the CLI and API used to be in the same codebase, and at times that meant that behavior is a bit split between "how the client handles it" and what the API handles. In this case; the `docker stop` command acting as synchronous (stay attached / wait until the container exits), but the actual stop isn't (really) (once signaled, the process is set in motion).  In this case, that also somewhat "masked" the issue. 

We can perhaps improve some of this; we were considering we could add an `?detach=true` query-parameter, which make the endpoint more clearly asynchronous (and a client can call the `/wait` endpoint to wait after that). Either way, that would be for a follow-up :sweat_smile:

I got caught up in other work today, but will continue work on my PR (cleaning up / improving the test :sweat_smile:)

review_comments: Been going back-and-forth whether to remove the context.Context here, but decided to go for the most minimal changes to fix the regression to reduce code-churn (and we may want to have the context available here in future for other purposes).
